entries.title: SSH
entries.summary: SSH provides encrypted remote shells, command execution, tunnelling and file transfer.
entries.significance: SSH often connects administrator workstations, jump hosts and production systems. Attackers value it because valid credentials or keys can provide quiet remote execution without introducing a new protocol. See the [defensive reference](https://man.openbsd.org/sshd) for the authoritative model. Password spraying, stolen private keys and exposed internet listeners are common concerns. Tunnels can also hide access to internal services inside an otherwise legitimate encrypted session. Defender view: Establish who owns the service, which assets should initiate it and which identities are allowed to complete sensitive operations.
triage: Firewall and flow records showing source, destination, timing and session duration.
`sshd` authentication records showing accepted and failed methods, account names and source addresses.
Session records such as `systemd-logind`, audit or shell telemetry linking a login to subsequent processes.
New or changed `authorized_keys` files, SSH configuration and host keys.
Port-forwarding or long-lived low-volume sessions that do not match the host's normal administrative pattern.
entries.caveats: Do not identify SSH from port 22 alone. Confirm the listening process and protocol handshake. SSH can use any port, while a different application can listen on 22. An accepted login proves authentication, not malicious intent. Compare the source, account, key fingerprint, time and follow-on processes with the approved access path.
